lessonTitle: Therapeutic Index and Drug Monitoring: Narrow Margins and Therapeutic Drug Monitoring

blocks.text: A 58-year-old man who has taken lithium for years for bipolar disorder develops a stomach bug, stops drinking, and becomes dehydrated. Within days he is tremulous, unsteady and confused. His dose never changed, yet his blood level crossed from therapeutic to toxic. For a few drugs the gap between a helpful and a harmful concentration is so narrow that levels must be measured.

blocks.markdown: The **therapeutic index (TI)** is a measure of how wide the margin is between the dose that produces a therapeutic effect and the dose that produces toxicity. It is derived from **quantal dose-response curves**, which record the proportion of a population showing an all-or-none response (effect, or toxicity) at each dose, unlike graded curves that measure the size of a response in one individual.

blocks.title: Therapeutic index and certain safety factor
blocks.text: Therapeutic index = TD50 / ED50, where TD50 is the dose producing a toxic effect in 50% of subjects and ED50 is the dose producing the desired effect in 50%. In animal studies the lethal dose LD50 is used in place of TD50. A larger index means a wider margin. The certain safety factor = TD1 / ED99 compares the dose that is toxic in 1% with the dose that is effective in 99%, and is more conservative because it considers the overlap of the curves.

blocks.caption: Doses must be in the same units. A certain safety factor below 1 means the curves overlap: some patients are toxic at doses that are not yet effective in everybody.

blocks.title: Calculating therapeutic index and safety factor
blocks.prompt: For drug P, 50% of patients respond at 30 mg (ED50) and 50% show toxicity at 90 mg (TD50). The dose effective in 99% (ED99) is 80 mg and the dose toxic in 1% (TD1) is 40 mg. Calculate TI and the certain safety factor, and interpret them. (Illustrative numbers.)

steps.text: A TI of 3 suggests a modest margin, and a certain safety factor of 0.5 means that doses effective in 99% of patients would be toxic in more than 1% of patients: the response curves overlap.
Conclusion: this drug has a narrow therapeutic margin and requires careful dose titration and monitoring.

blocks.answer: TI = 3; certain safety factor = 0.5 (overlapping curves, narrow margin)

blocks.markdown: **Limits of the therapeutic index.** The TI is a population statistic from animal or trial data and does not describe an individual patient. It ignores the **severity** of the toxic effect (a mild rash versus death), the **slopes** of the effect and toxicity curves (two drugs with the same TI can differ greatly in how quickly risk rises with dose), and variation in individuals caused by age, renal function or interacting drugs. LD50-based values from animals may not translate to humans. In clinical practice, a **therapeutic range** (or window) of plasma concentration, which varies by laboratory and guideline, is used instead, and drugs with a narrow range are said to have a narrow therapeutic index.

blocks.caption: Examples of narrow therapeutic index drugs and why monitoring is needed.
rows: Renally cleared; levels rise with dehydration, NSAIDs, ACE inhibitors
Renally cleared; toxicity increased by hypokalaemia
Variable absorption; transplant outcomes depend on level

blocks.title: Three narrow-index drugs to remember
blocks.text: Warfarin, digoxin and lithium (also phenytoin, gentamicin, theophylline, ciclosporin) have narrow therapeutic indices. Small changes in dose, clearance or interacting drugs can move a patient from ineffective to toxic.

blocks.markdown: **Therapeutic drug monitoring (TDM)** means measuring drug concentrations to individualise dosing. It is indicated when: the drug has a narrow therapeutic index; there is a clear relationship between concentration and effect or toxicity; there is large inter-individual variability in pharmacokinetics; clinical effect is hard to measure; toxicity or non-adherence is suspected; or kidney, liver function or interacting drugs have changed. It is not useful when the effect itself can be easily measured (for example blood pressure or blood glucose) or when there is no concentration-effect relationship.

blocks.title: Deciding when to sample
blocks.prompt: A drug with a half-life of 12 hours is started at a fixed regular dose. When should the first trough level be taken to judge the steady-state level, and why take a trough?

steps.text: Steady state is reached after about 4 to 5 half-lives. With a half-life of 12 h this is 48 to 60 h, so the first level is taken at about 60 h (2.5 days).

Sample just before the next dose (the trough). The trough is the lowest and most reproducible point in the dosing interval and reflects the elimination phase, with no confusion from absorption or distribution.
Record the timing: time of last dose and time of sample, since a level taken at the wrong time can mislead.
Exceptions: digoxin is sampled at least 6 hours after a dose to allow tissue distribution; lithium is sampled about 12 hours post dose; for toxicity suspected clinically, sample immediately.

blocks.answer: First trough at about 60 h, immediately before the next dose, with times recorded

items: Sample at steady state (4 to 5 half-lives) unless toxicity is suspected, when samples are taken immediately.
Trough (pre-dose) levels are usual for drugs such as vancomycin, phenytoin and ciclosporin; digoxin needs at least 6 hours post-dose; lithium about 12 hours post-dose.
Interpret the level with the clinical picture and renal function; treat the patient, not the number.
Repeat levels after dose changes, new interacting drugs, or illness that affects clearance.

blocks.title: Timing matters
blocks.text: A digoxin level taken one hour after a dose will appear falsely high because the drug has not yet distributed to tissues. Always record when the dose was given and when the sample was taken.

points: Therapeutic index = TD50 / ED50 (and certain safety factor = TD1 / ED99); it is a population measure that ignores severity of toxicity, curve slopes and individual variation.
Narrow therapeutic index drugs include warfarin, digoxin, lithium, phenytoin, gentamicin and ciclosporin.
TDM is indicated for narrow-index, variable-kinetics drugs, usually sampled at steady state before the next dose (trough), with specific timing for digoxin and lithium.

questions.stem: How is the therapeutic index defined?

options.text: TD50 divided by ED50
ED50 divided by TD50
The maximum dose divided by the minimum dose
The half-life divided by the clearance

distractorRationale.a: Correct: the ratio of the median toxic dose to the median effective dose.
distractorRationale.c: Incorrect: this is not a defined index.

questions.explanation: The therapeutic index compares the dose that causes toxicity in half of subjects with the dose that is effective in half. A larger ratio means a wider safety margin.

questions.stem: In an animal study, the LD50 of a drug is 120 mg/kg and the ED50 is 4 mg/kg. Calculate the therapeutic index (LD50 / ED50).
questions.explanation: TI = LD50 / ED50 = 120 / 4 = 30. This suggests a wide margin in the animal, though such values cannot be assumed to apply to humans.

questions.stem: For a drug, the dose toxic in 1% of patients (TD1) is 60 mg and the dose effective in 99% of patients (ED99) is 40 mg. Calculate the certain safety factor (TD1 / ED99).
questions.explanation: Certain safety factor = 60 / 40 = 1.5. A value above 1 means that the dose effective in 99% is lower than the dose toxic in 1%, so the curves do not overlap at their extremes.

questions.stem: Which is a recognised limitation of the therapeutic index as a safety measure?

options.text: It does not take account of the severity of the toxic effect or the steepness of the dose-response curves
It requires the drug to be given intravenously
It can only be calculated for antibiotics
It describes an individual patient exactly

questions.correctOptionText: It does not take account of the severity of the toxic effect or the steepness of the dose-response curves

distractorRationale.a: Correct: two drugs with the same ratio may differ greatly in the seriousness of toxicity and in how fast risk rises.
distractorRationale.c: Incorrect: it is applied to any drug.
distractorRationale.d: Incorrect: it is a population statistic.

questions.explanation: The index is a ratio of two median doses and ignores how serious the toxicity is and how the curves are shaped. It also reflects populations, not an individual's pharmacokinetics.

questions.stem: Which list contains only drugs with a narrow therapeutic index?

options.text: Warfarin, digoxin and lithium
Amoxicillin, paracetamol and simvastatin
Omeprazole, cetirizine and salbutamol
Vitamin C, ibuprofen and loperamide

distractorRationale.a: Correct: all three have small margins between therapeutic and toxic levels.
distractorRationale.b: Incorrect: these have wider margins at usual doses.
distractorRationale.c: Incorrect: wide margins at usual doses.

questions.explanation: Warfarin, digoxin and lithium are the classical narrow therapeutic index drugs, requiring monitoring of INR or serum level. Small dose or clearance changes can cause toxicity or treatment failure.

questions.stem: For which of the following is therapeutic drug monitoring most appropriate?

options.text: Gentamicin in a patient with changing renal function
Amlodipine for hypertension
Simvastatin for hypercholesterolaemia
Cetirizine for hay fever

questions.correctOptionText: Gentamicin in a patient with changing renal function

distractorRationale.a: Correct: narrow index, renal clearance, toxicity risk and variable kinetics.
distractorRationale.b: Incorrect: effect is monitored through blood pressure.
distractorRationale.c: Incorrect: effect monitored by lipids; no concentration monitoring needed.
distractorRationale.d: Incorrect: wide margin and clinical effect is easily judged.

questions.explanation: TDM is useful when a drug has a narrow margin, variable clearance and clear concentration-toxicity relationship, as with gentamicin. For drugs with easily measured effects or wide margins it adds little.

questions.stem: A patient with heart failure on digoxin is suspected of toxicity because of nausea and visual disturbance. A level is drawn 2 hours after the last oral dose. How should it be interpreted?

options.text: It may be falsely high because digoxin has not yet distributed into tissues, so it should be interpreted with the timing and clinical picture
It is the ideal timing for a digoxin level
It is falsely low because digoxin is already eliminated
Timing does not matter for digoxin

questions.correctOptionText: It may be falsely high because digoxin has not yet distributed into tissues, so it should be interpreted with the timing and clinical picture

distractorRationale.a: Correct: digoxin takes several hours to distribute, so early levels overestimate the tissue-equilibrated concentration.
distractorRationale.b: Incorrect: at least 6 hours post-dose is advised.

questions.explanation: Digoxin has a prolonged distribution phase, so samples within about 6 hours of a dose overestimate the concentration at the tissue receptor. Where toxicity is suspected, a level may still be taken, but it must be interpreted with its timing and the clinical picture.

questions.stem: A narrow-index drug has a half-life of 12 hours and is started at a fixed regular dose. Taking 5 half-lives as the time to steady state, how many hours after starting should the first steady-state trough level be taken?
questions.explanation: 5 x 12 h = 60 h. The sample is taken immediately before the next dose (trough), when the concentration is lowest and most reproducible.

questions.stem: Define the therapeutic index and discuss why it is an imperfect measure of the safety of a drug in clinical practice.
markingGuide: Definition: TD50 / ED50 (or LD50 / ED50 in animals); ratio of median toxic dose to median effective dose; larger = wider margin
Ignores the severity of the toxic effect
Ignores slopes of the curves and overlap; certain safety factor TD1 / ED99 is more conservative
Population statistic: individual variation (age, renal function, interactions) and animal LD50 may not translate to humans
In practice the therapeutic range and monitoring are used for narrow index drugs
questions.explanation: The index summarises two median doses and ignores the shape and variability of the curves and the seriousness of harm. It is therefore a guide, not a guarantee of safety.

questions.stem: State three drugs with a narrow therapeutic index and explain when therapeutic drug monitoring is indicated and how samples should be timed.
markingGuide: Three narrow-index drugs, for example warfarin, digoxin, lithium (also phenytoin, gentamicin, ciclosporin)
TDM indicated for narrow index, clear concentration-effect relationship, large pharmacokinetic variability, hard-to-measure clinical effect
Also when toxicity or non-adherence is suspected, or renal/hepatic function or interacting drugs change
Sample at steady state (4 to 5 half-lives) unless toxicity is suspected
Trough sampling just before the next dose for most drugs; digoxin at least 6 h post-dose; lithium about 12 h post-dose
Record dose and sample times and interpret with the clinical picture
questions.explanation: Monitoring is useful where the concentration relates to effect and kinetics vary between patients. Correct timing is essential, because a wrongly timed level can mislead dosing.
